title: The research for new, natural food dyes - NewsBreak
text:
By Lauren Soulek ,
1 hours ago
BROOKINGS, S.D. (KELO) – Red 40, Red 3, Yellow 5, Blue 1 and other synthetic food dyes have come under a lot of scrutiny in recent years over potential health concerns. Over the last few months, the Trump Administration has called for a phase-out of many of these dyes by the end of next year.
Nikki Gronli running for SD’s US House seat But what could replace those dyes?
SDSU’s Dr. Ananda Nanjundaswamy is creating a possible replacement for synthetic food dyes at a Dakota BioWorx lab in Brookings. In order to make it, he’s growing microbes in bioreactors.
“So, they (microbes) are present everywhere, especially on the plant surfaces, fruit surfaces. We found that when they are in the lab condition, by providing optimal conditions, they can grow very well and produce this compote,” Nanjundaswamy said. “And they can, the immediate requirement is to provide a replacement for synthetic red dye 3 and then eventually we might replace these things with other colors also.”
A lot of natural food dyes stem from plants, but Nanjundaswamy says his process of using microbes is more efficient.
“Tomato, for example, it takes about 90 days for it to grow and mature. There are so many things that might happen in that 90 days, but in case of microbes, you can control pretty much everything — temperature, you can control nutrition and you can control other microorganisms entering there,” Nanjundaswamy said. “So, pretty much you can allow them to grow in an ideal condition. So, while plant takes what 90 days to make, microbes can make it in two days and three days. In fact, this one we made in less than 40 hours.”
Nanjundaswamy’s team is now working towards a patent and commercial-scale production of this product, which could mean a lot for South Dakota.
“For the state, that creates new business or new capacities in existing business. And these businesses hire our graduates, South Dakota’s young people,” Daniel Scholl, Vice President of Research and Economic Development at SDSU, said. “They provide a reason for young people to stay and develop their careers here, build the society, build an economy.”
Nanjundaswamy says on top of the color properties of the microbes, they also have prebiotic and antioxidant properties that could add nutrients to the foods they color.
